```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
# quarto doesn't find my files in nested folder structure, 
# doctor google recommends this code from the "here" package, which works.

h1 <- utils::read.csv(here::here("data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv"))
h2 <- utils::read.csv(here::here("data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv"))
```



```{r}

# small data fix

# I realized that my boxplot labelled the x-axis wrong, so I need to changes the levels in my cot_politics variable
# For the sake of simplicity, I will just do this here.

h1$cot_politics <- factor(h1$cot_politics, levels = c("far_left", "center_left", "center", "center_right", "far_right"))

```

## Hypothesis 1

Self-reported physical attractivness differs depending on individuals
political beliefs.

### Variables and descriptive statistics

- **Political beliefs (`cot_politics`):** Categorical variable with
  three groups: "far_left", "center_left", "center", "center_right",
  far_right".
- **Physical attractivenes (`self_phsysatt`):** Numerical variable with
  self reported point rating of individuals physical attractivness on a
  scale from 1 to 11, where 1 is very low and 11 is very high.

```{r}
#| label: h1-descriptives
# Count respondents in each group.
table(h1$cot_politics)

# Summarize attractiveness points seperately in each group.
by(h1$self_physatt, h1$cot_politics, summary)

```

#fig-distr shows the distribution of observations of political beliefs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distr
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Political Beliefs"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

# 2. Generate the plot
ggplot(h1, aes(x = cot_politics)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Political Beliefs",
    x = "Political Beliefs",
    y = "Count (Number of Observations)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
           scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Far Left", "Center Left", "Center", "Center Right", "Far Right")) +# Clean theme with readable font size
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()  
      # Removes vertical gridlines for cleaner look
  )
```

### Graph

@fig-pol-att shows the distribution shows the distribution of
self-reported physical attractivness score by political beliefs. The
boxplot shows the median and quartiles with a central box, while the
whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values within a specified
range, and individual points plotted beyond them show the outliers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pol-att
#| fig-cap: "Self Reported Physical Attractiveness and Political Beliefs"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5


# plot
ggplot(data = h1, aes(x = cot_politics,
                   y = self_physatt,
                   fill = cot_politics)) +
         geom_boxplot(width = .4) + 
         labs(x = "Political Beliefs", 
         y = "(Self reported) Physical Attractiveness Scale",, 
         title = "Self Reported Physical Attractiveness and Political Beliefs") +
         scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Far Left", "Center Left", "Center", "Center Right", "Far Right")) +
         guides(fill = "none") 

```

### Observed trend

summary(h1)

```{r}
#| label: h1_anovas

model <- aov(self_physatt ~ cot_politics, data = h1)
summary(model)

# Pairwise comparisons
TukeyHSD(model)


```

The ANOVA results indicate a statistically significant difference in
self-reported physical attractiveness across political belief groups
(F(4, 83139) = 95.58, p \< .001). Tukey post-hoc comparisons show most
political beliefs group differ significantly from each other and that
far-right respondents tend to report higher physical attractiveness than
all other groups, while far-left and center-left respondents do not
differ significantly. Overall, individuals with right-wing beliefs tend
to report higher physical attractiveness.

## Hypothesis 2

Importance of looking attractive has a positive effect on daily time
spent enhancing appearance .

### Variables and descriptive statistics

- **Importance of Own Attractivness (`Attract_importance_1`):**
  Numerical variable with self reported importance of own attractivness
  on a scale from 1 to 9, where 1 is not at all important and 9 is
  extremely important.
- **Daily time spent enhancing appearance (`app_enh_total`):** Composite
  numerical score, sum of 8 variables of time spent on: make up
  (`Time_A_makeup_1`), hygiene (`Time_A_hyg_1`), cosmetics
  (`Time_A_cosm_1`), exercise (`Time_A_exercise_1`), hair
  (`Time_A_hair_1`), dressing up (`Time_A_dress_1`), diet
  (`Time_A_diet_1`), other appearance enhancing activities
  (`Time_A_other_1`). Score is the sum of minutes spent per day for each
  activity. Higher value indicate higher overall daily time spent
  enhancing appearances. Item value 360 represents 6 hours or more.

```{r}
#| label: h2-descriptives
# don't show ID here
summary(h2[, c("attract_importance_1", "app_enh_total")])

```

### Graph

@fig-attenh illustrates the relationship between the time spent
enhancing an individual's appearance and the importance of their own
physical appearance. The data are visualized using a scatter plot paired
with a linear regression line that summarizes the overall trend.
Individual data points are jittered to prevent overlapping and improve
readability, though the underlying recorded scores remain unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: fig-attenh
#| fig-cap: "Time Spent Enhancing Appearance in Relation to Importance of Appearance"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

#Scatter Plot with line
ggplot(data = h2, 
                  aes(x = attract_importance_1,
                      y = app_enh_total)) +
                         geom_jitter(width=.12, height=.1, alpha=.2, size = .6)  +
        labs(x = "Reported Importance Of Own Attractivness", 
        y = "Composite Score of Daily Time Spent Enhancing Appearance (min)", 
        title = "Time Spent Enhancing Appearance in Relation to Importance of Appearance") +
  geom_smooth(method="lm")



```

### Observed trend

```{r}
#| label: correlation
r <- cor(h2$attract_importance_1, h2$app_enh_total, use = "complete.obs")
round(r,2)


```

A correlation coefficient of `{r} round(r, 2)` indicates a weak,
positive linear relationship between the two variables. Respondents who
reported more confidence in finding a new partner tended to report lower
commitment. Individuals who place greater importance on their physical
appearance tend to spend slightly more time enhancing it, though this
tendency is small.
